title: How omxcode fits together
subtitle: One struct describes the screen; each platform's own toolkit draws it, and an agent reads the same description

floors.label: Mojo
floors.note: one binary: your app and omxcode

floors.label: already there
floors.note: each platform's own toolkit, and an agent

nodes.label: update()
nodes.desc: Runs when something happens. It gets an Event that carries a message number (TAP) and changes the fields. It never touches a widget.

nodes.label: state
nodes.desc: The app's state is just the struct's fields: var taps: Int. Only update() changes them.

nodes.label: view()
nodes.desc: Reads the state and returns what the screen should be: a column with a title, a line and a button. It is called again after every update().

nodes.label: Runtime
nodes.desc: mojoui/app.mojo. Takes an Event from any host or from the agent, calls update(), then view(), then diff(), and keeps the tree that is on screen now.

nodes.label: View tree
nodes.desc: view() returns data, not widgets: a flat list of Nodes (mojoui/view.mojo). Each one has a kind (BUTTON, FIELD, TOGGLE…), its text, the message number it sends, a tag and a tooltip. Every host and the agent read this one description.

nodes.label: diff()
nodes.desc: mojoui/diff.mojo. Compares the new tree with the one on screen. Same shape: a few patches (set this text, this value). Otherwise only the part that changed is rebuilt.

nodes.label: GTK 4
nodes.desc: Mojo calls GTK's own C functions directly (about 1,160 calls in mojoui/hosts/gtk.mojo): gtk_button_new_with_label. GTK calls back into a Mojo function when a button is clicked. No C bridge, one native binary.

nodes.label: AppKit
nodes.desc: Mojo sends Objective-C messages itself and registers its own class to receive taps: real NSButtons. Runs on GitHub's macOS machines; wide screens still have a layout bug.

nodes.label: Browser
nodes.desc: The Mojo app loads into the web host (Python, FastHTML) as a module. The host sends real <button>, <input> and <select> elements, so the browser draws its own controls.

nodes.label: Android
nodes.desc: Mojo drives Android's own views through JNI; one 78-line Java file forwards taps back. Runs on the emulator.

nodes.label: A person
nodes.desc: Sees each platform's own controls, not a drawn imitation of them.

nodes.label: Agent host
nodes.desc: mojoui/hosts/agent.py, an MCP server. It reads the same tree and makes one tool per control: the tag (or the text) is the tool's name, the tooltip its description, the kind its arguments (a toggle takes on, a field takes text). It runs the app in its own session, or attaches to a running window.

nodes.label: An agent
nodes.desc: Gets the tools and a text outline of the screen. It calls tools; it never has to find a button in a screenshot.

steps.note: The app's state is its struct's fields. Here: taps = 0.
view() reads the state and describes the screen: a title, a line, a button.
It returns data, not widgets. The button is one node: BUTTON, "Tap me", sends TAP.
Nothing is on screen yet, so every node is new.
On Linux, Mojo calls GTK's own C function: gtk_button_new_with_label.
On a Mac, the same node becomes an NSButton, through objc_msgSend.
On the web, a real <button> element.
On Android, an Android button, through JNI.
Each person gets their platform's own controls. Nobody drew a button.
You tap the button. GTK calls a Mojo function directly.
The host finds the button's node and sends its message: an Event with TAP.
The runtime hands the Event to update().
taps becomes 1.
view() describes the screen again, from the new state.
A new tree. Only one line's text is different.
diff() compares it with the tree on screen and finds one change.
One patch: set that label's text. Nothing else is touched.
The agent host reads the same tree. Every control becomes a tool: this button is tap-me.
The agent gets the tools and a text outline of the screen. No pixels to read.
It calls the tool tap-me.
The call becomes the same Event a tap sends: TAP.
update() can't tell an agent from a person. Nobody wrote an API for the agent.
The screen changes the same way it does for a tap.
The tools follow the screen: when it changes, the agent is told its list changed.
